title: A mysterious hermit
caption: The irregular dwarf galaxy UGC 4879, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: UGC 4879 · constellation Ursa Major · about 4 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A scattered drizzle of stars across this Hubble image makes up the galaxy UGC 4879. It is an irregular dwarf galaxy, a type that is smaller and messier than most, without the sweeping swirl of a spiral or the tidy shape of an elliptical.

UGC 4879 is also very isolated. Its nearest neighbour, Leo A, is about 2.3 million light years away, roughly the gap between the Andromeda Galaxy and the Milky Way. Because it has not interacted with other galaxies, it offers a clean laboratory for studying how stars form without outside disturbance.

Its history is puzzling. Studies show a lot of star formation in the first 4 billion years after the Big Bang, then a strange lull of nine billion years with little star birth, ending with a fresh burst that began 1 billion years ago. Why it behaved this way is still unknown.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (3.32 x 2.47 arcminutes) and distance (4 million light years), the frame spans roughly 3,900 × 2,900 light-years. Its light set out about 4 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, using filters at 606 and 814 nm, in visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves the galaxy's individual stars, which would blur into a faint smudge through a small telescope.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Because UGC 4879 has not interacted with any surrounding galaxies, its star formation is not complicated by outside influences, which makes it a useful laboratory for astronomers trying to understand how starbirth works across the Universe.
alt: A loose, irregular scattering of stars forming a small dwarf galaxy.
